extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies, agency counsel, OPM staff, labor unions, employee advocates, and legal practitioners participating in notice-and-comment rulemaking on civil service protections
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of substantive legal and regulatory standards from OPM's final rule preamble responding to public comments about retention of civil service status, removal protections, and excepted-service scheduling under Title 5. Focuses on criteria used to interpret statutes, precedent, and agency authority in personnel actions and schedule designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of accrued competitive-service status upon involuntary move
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees in the competitive or excepted service retain rights previously accrued upon an involuntary move from the competitive service to the excepted service, or from one excepted-service schedule to another, unless the employee relinquishes such rights by voluntarily encumbering a position that explicitly results in a loss of, or different, rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM amends 5 CFR part 752 and part 212 to clarify this long-standing interpretation. Historical authorities (e.g., Roth v. Brownell, Executive Order 10577, CSC/OPM guidance across administrations) support that incumbents retain removal protections when their occupied positions are redesignated. The rule treats agency-initiated movements (rescheduling/reassignment/conversion initiated by the agency) as involuntary and not affecting accrued rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary versus involuntary movement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary movement is generally characterized by an employee initiating a reassignment, conversion, or transfer by pursuing and accepting an offer to serve in a different position; an agency-initiated move of the position is regarded as involuntary with respect to the incumbent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether movement extinguishes accrued rights depends on circumstances: voluntary acceptance of a new appointment can extinguish prior accrued rights (especially where the new appointment explicitly notifies the appointee), whereas involuntary agency-initiated moves should not affect previously accrued rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'employee' for adverse action entitlement under 5 U.S.C. 7501 and 7511
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of who qualifies as an 'employee' for purposes of adverse action procedures in subchapters I and II of chapter 75, and which employees are covered by non-appealable adverse actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM relies on 5 U.S.C. 7501 and 7511 and relevant Federal Circuit precedent to conform regulatory text (parts 752 and 212) with statutory language and to clarify coverage; OPM may prescribe regulations under 5 U.S.C. 7504 and 7514 to carry out subchapters I and II respectively (with MSPB-prescribed exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to appeal rights for performance-based actions under chapter 43
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance-based actions under chapter 43 and related eligibility/processes are governed by 5 U.S.C. 4303; section 4303(e) defines when an employee is entitled to MSPB appeal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 43 cross-references chapter 75 for appeal eligibility; employees who are preference eligible, in the competitive service, or covered by subchapter II and removed under section 4303 are entitled to appeal to the MSPB under 5 U.S.C. 7701. OPM may issue regulations to carry out subchapter I of chapter 43 under 5 U.S.C. 4305.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) determinations be made before appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination under 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) that a position is 'confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating' must be made before the employee is appointed to the position for the exception to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSPB precedent requires pre-appointment determinations; agencies must follow applicable procedures when making such determinations. Improper or after-the-fact determinations (or attempts to use redesignation to circumvent protections) can be invalidated (e.g., Blalock v. Department of Agriculture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees can acquire a property interest in their positions under chapter 75
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees can earn a property interest in their positions once they satisfy probationary/trial periods or the durational requirement of current continuous service under 5 U.S.C. 7511, and these property interests are protected upon involuntary moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is supported by Supreme Court precedent and historical enactments (Veterans Preference Act, Ramspeck Act). Commenters and OPM cite case law (Roth and progeny) and administrative practice indicating vested rights cannot be removed by executive action without due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority to impose removal restrictions on inferior officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may constitutionally provide removal restrictions for inferior officers; inferior officer status does not inherently require at-will removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and Supreme Court cases (United States v. Perkins; Morrison v. Olson; United States v. Arthrex, Inc.; and discussion of Free Enterprise Fund and its progeny) show that removal limitations for inferior officers—when accompanied by oversight and review—have been sustained. Arthrex confirms inferior officers can have removal restrictions if subject to review by a superior accountable to the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between PCAOB-style removal restrictions and civil service removal protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal protections at issue in Free Enterprise Fund (e.g., PCAOB inferior officers removable only for specified willful violations) are materially more stringent than the civil service system's removal standards, which allow removal for 'the efficiency of the service' and oversight by other Executive Branch officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free Enterprise Fund's majority opinion distinguished civil service protections from the PCAOB regime and stated nothing cast doubt on use of the civil service system within independent agencies. Comparisons that ignore the difference in degree of restrictions are legally flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPM's authority to define statutory terms and promulgate regulations clarifying exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OPM is authorized by Congress and the President throughout title 5 to regulate the civil service and carry out the purposes of civil service statutes, including issuing definitions and clarifying the scope of exceptions like 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking can be based on longstanding legislative history, legal precedent, and past practice; issuing regulations does not prevent a President from creating excepted service schedules but clarifies statutory language and intended scope of exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescheduling cannot be used to bypass civil service protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not employ rescheduling (moving positions to excepted service schedules) as a means to eliminate accrued civil service procedural protections for incumbents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM's regulatory amendments aim to reduce the risk of misapplying civil service statutes by using rescheduling to bypass protections. Historical decisions and guidance (Roth, CSC/OPM memoranda) support that incumbents retain protections despite rescheduling unless they voluntarily waive them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When statutory exception or pre-appointment determination applies to new appointees
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress statutorily excepts a position from the competitive service or an agency head properly declares a position policy-influencing before appointment, future appointees may lack chapter 75 procedural protections for those appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Stanley v. Department of Justice demonstrate that intervening determinations made before new appointments can affect rights of appointees to subsequent terms; the timing of the determination and the nature (statutory exception vs. later declaration) are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity of non-appealable adverse action regulation with statutory language and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation governing non-appealable adverse actions should conform to statutory language in 5 U.S.C. 7501 and to Federal Circuit precedent to clarify which employees are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM amends regulatory text to align with statutory definitions and case law to reduce uncertainty about coverage for short suspensions and non-appealable actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of functions preserve employee status and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees subject to transfers of functions that move them to other organizational entities (e.g., transfer to Peace Corps incident to transfer of functions) retain their competitive-service status and related protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogs and Comptroller General opinions support retention of status when movement is incident to transfer of functions rather than voluntary reappointment into an excepted regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on improper redesignation and improper use of RIF to avoid protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot bypass procedural protections by mischaracterizing actions—e.g., using a reduction-in-force (RIF) to eliminate Schedule A incumbents and then appointing them to Schedule C positions; such redesignations can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSPB decisions (e.g., Blalock) have rejected such agency claims, finding improper actions and directing reinstatement of preference-eligible employees separated without adherence to adverse action procedures.
